clue.text: Initially doctors diagnosed impetigo though it's only necessary to go on a supplement

indicators.note: initially points at the opening letter of each of the following words
one piece goes on, after, the next word of the clue, fixing the order of the parts

blocks.note: taken as written

blocks.clueFragment: doctors diagnosed impetigo though it's only necessary
blocks.note: first letters of these seven words

explanation.surface: A doctor treating a skin infection only needs to add a supplement to the patient's regime.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven initials are placed after the A, giving ADDITION; 'a supplement' looks like one phrase but the A is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An addition is something added on, which is exactly what a supplement is: a synonym.

clue.text: Novelist displaying range, putting character from best-seller in novel I hate

indicators.note: novel means new or fresh, so the letters it sits beside are made into a new order
putting one thing in another places it inside, with the word 'in' that follows

blocks.note: an Aga is a make of kitchen range, the big cast-iron cooker
letters to be rearranged
the Bible is said to be the best-selling book of all, and Christ is its central character

explanation.surface: A writer lets slip a dislike of a fellow author's best-selling novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The key leap is the Bible, often called the world's best-selling book, whose central figure sits inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie, author of the Poirot and Marple mysteries, is among the best-selling writers of fiction ever.

clue.text: Male getting into retro blue movies?

indicators.note: retro means looking backwards, so the word for blue is read the other way round

blocks.note: blue as in feeling low
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A man watching old-fashioned blue films, i.e. pornography.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue movies' reads as smut, but blue here means unhappy. The question mark flags that movies are only one kind of drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Dramas are plays or films telling a story, so movies are an example, signalled by the question mark.

clue.text: Make their lot sit out – now we're getting somewhere

indicators.note: out here means put out of order or disarranged, so these letters must be shuffled into another order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters used

explanation.surface: A frustrated teacher gets the whole class to sit down at last and feels progress is being made.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are spoken expressions of approval when things start to improve after a poor start.

clue.text: Occasionally force dog to come round

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: second and fourth letters
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: An owner occasionally has to use force to make the dog come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come round' suggests a dog returning or someone waking; here it means an event coming around, taking place.
explanation.definitionFit: To occur is to happen, and an event that comes round, like a birthday, takes place again.

clue.text: Practised what a famous Norman did using gilt iron

definitions.text: Practised what a famous Norman did

indicators.note: using here means taking in or consuming, so one element is absorbed inside the other

blocks.note: gilt is a thin coating of gold
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A famous Norman practising with a gilded iron club, as golfers do.
explanation.walkthrough: Greg Norman is an Australian golf champion; 'iron' fits his club, but it is the element FE placed in GOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Greg Norman was a professional golfer, so what he did, put into the past tense, is golfed.

clue.text: Unusually bourgeois lad ran union?

indicators.note: unusually suggests something done in an odd way, so these letters are set out in a strange new order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters used

explanation.surface: A middle-class young man unusually took charge of a trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: Organised labour means workers grouped in trade unions; a union is an example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Enjoyment of father joining it for a night to begin with

indicators.note: one thing for another means it takes the other's place, so one letter is swapped out
to begin with says the swap happens at the first matching place in the word

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, as for a priest
a union is a joining together
taken as written
N is an abbreviation for night; this is the letter swapped out

explanation.surface: A father enjoying the time he has for a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is the swap signal: only the first N of the joining word is replaced, the second stays.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruition is an old word for enjoyment or pleasure in possessing something, before its usual sense of fulfilment.

clue.text: Keep moving home following clinical condition

indicators.note: moving means shifting position, so the word before it has its letters rearranged
following says this part comes after the other in the answer

blocks.note: a detached is a house standing alone, in estate-agent shorthand

explanation.surface: Someone keeps moving house after being diagnosed with an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep moving home' reads as relocating repeatedly; it is RETAIN rearranged, placed after the word for a type of house.
explanation.definitionFit: A detached retina is a medical emergency where the light-sensitive layer of the eye peels away.

clue.text: Page's title after being edited down

indicators.note: editing down trims the ends off text, so only an inner run of letters is kept

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A page's heading after editors have cut it down.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is read as 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf is a single sheet of a book, giving two pages, so the words serve as synonyms.

clue.text: No time to teach naval manoeuvres in flood

indicators.note: no time means the letter for time, T, is dropped from the word it applies to
manoeuvres are movements and repositionings, so the letters are moved into new places

blocks.note: the word with its T for time removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: There's no time to teach sailors how to manoeuvre during a flood.
explanation.definitionFit: An avalanche is figuratively an overwhelming flood or deluge of something, such as letters or complaints.

clue.text: Smallest amount of gin and relative's wasted

indicators.note: the smallest amount of a word is just a single letter of it, its opening one

blocks.note: first letter
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: Just a drop of gin and a relative is wasted, i.e. drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' reads as drunk, after the gin; here it means emaciated.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaunt means thin and haggard, as someone wasted by illness or hunger looks.

clue.text: Republican pursuing House seat getting increasingly gruff

indicators.note: pursuing means coming after, so this part goes at the end

blocks.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
seat as in backside, British slang
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican chasing a seat in the House of Representatives grows hoarse from campaigning.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface hides a rude meaning: seat is the backside, ARSE in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoarser is the comparative of hoarse, rough-voiced, so it describes a voice becoming more gruff.

clue.text: Maniac putting a jerk on air

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is placed next to it, after it here

blocks.note: to fan is to air or cool something
taken as written
a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: A maniac broadcasting a jerky performance on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanatic is someone with obsessive zeal, which is also a sense of maniac: an enthusiast taken to excess.

clue.text: Ancient artefact and Villa's location protected by political favour?

explanation.surface: A valuable artefact kept at a villa under political patronage.
explanation.walkthrough: Villa means the football club Aston Villa, not a house; a favour is a ribbon or badge worn as a token.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rosetta Stone is the ancient Egyptian inscribed slab that helped decipher hieroglyphs, now in the British Museum.

clue.text: Ultimately score after extra time

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of each of the next words counts

blocks.note: last letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A football match where the winner finally scores after extra time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra time' looks like a single football phrase, but 'time' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a period of time, so the two are synonyms in crosswords and everyday speech.

clue.text: Defeat regularly upset supporter?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is taken
in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from the bottom up

blocks.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A sports fan upset by a defeat that keeps happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' points to a fan, but it means something that holds up a golf ball, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A tee is the small peg that holds a golf ball up before driving, so it literally supports it.

clue.text: I need a hand with driving on vacation – somehow revealing ulterior motive

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like someone emptying out basements, but the first word is a verb of jumping and the second a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb meaning leaps over and a plural noun for arched underground storerooms.

clue.text: See 8
Fancy, fashionable picture frames

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective for the frames; it is the verb, and the picture word goes around the fashionable one.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something can mean to suppose or picture it in the mind, as imagining does.

clue.text: Memory of niece's school essentially

the two central letters of the six

clue.text: Fizzy tea? It's absurd

explanation.walkthrough: The fizzy word comes second in the answer though first in the clue.
